title: Violence Flares Again in Thailand’s Deep South
gist: Andrew Nachemson reports from Narathiwat and Pattani that the Malay Muslim separatist insurgency in Thailand's deep south is escalating again, with Deep South Watch counting 523 casualties from 608 incidents in 2025 versus 335 incidents in 2020, a July checkpoint attack and 50+ coordinated infrastructure strikes in August. Locals expect further deterioration under the new nationalist, pro-military Bhumjaithai government as stalled peace talks, martial-law dragnets and closed political space push youth toward the BRN.

insights.claim: A July 2026 gun-and-pipe-bomb attack on a security checkpoint in Thailand's Narathiwat province killed five Thai Rangers and injured six civilians, and was followed in August by more than 50 coordinated attacks mainly targeting government offices, telecom towers and railways.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Insurgents are deliberately targeting telecom and rail infrastructure in southern Thailand, a direct operational risk for operators there.

insights.claim: According to Deep South Watch, violence in southern Thailand ebbed to 116 deaths and 161 injuries from 335 incidents in 2020, but rose to 523 casualties from 608 incidents by 2025.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: A near-doubling of incidents since 2020 marks a clear trend reversal in a long-running security risk for Thailand.
insights.quote: By 2025, these figures had increased again to 523 casualties from 608 incidents.

insights.claim: Deep South Watch head Srisompob Jitpiromsri says the BRN appears to observe a 'ceiling' on violence, aiming to pressure the Thai government without provoking an extreme response, which is why the August infrastructure attacks reportedly caused no deaths.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Calibrated, infrastructure-focused violence suggests a persistent low-grade risk rather than a mass-casualty spiral, unless the state overreacts.

insights.claim: The Barisan Revolusi Nasional, the largest armed separatist group in Thailand's deep south, is relatively decentralized, with much of its leadership based in Malaysia and local units largely operating on their own.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: A decentralized structure with cross-border leadership makes negotiated settlement harder and implicates Thailand-Malaysia relations.
insights.quote: Much of the BRN’s leadership is based in Malaysia, with field commanders in Thailand, and many local units broadly operate on their own.
insights.locator: The armed movement is relatively decentralized

insights.claim: The insurgency traces to Siam's 1786 seizure of the Patani Sultanate and a 1909 treaty with colonial Britain, and Thai nation-building rooted in Buddhist cultural norms has failed in the far south, where ethnic Malay Muslims are about 80 percent of the population.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Deep identity-based grievances imply the conflict is structural and unlikely to be resolved quickly.

insights.claim: The BRN relaunched the insurgency in 2004 when a power struggle between Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra and the military weakened control of the south, and Human Rights Watch recorded nearly 2,400 deaths in the first three and a half years, nearly 2,200 of them civilians.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Elite power struggles in Bangkok have historically opened windows for southern escalation.
insights.locator: The separatist movement in southern Thailand

insights.claim: Thailand's three southernmost provinces have been under some form of martial law or emergency decree since 2004, and martial law lets the military detain suspects without charge for up to 37 days.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Two decades of emergency rule signal entrenched governance and human-rights risk in the region.
insights.quote: Martial law in the region allows the military to detain suspects without charge for up to 37 days.

insights.claim: Islamic school vice president Muhammad Hayeewaehama estimates 80 percent of ethnic Malay Muslims in the region send their children to religious schools, which the Thai government has pressured since the 1980s to adopt the state curriculum.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: State-led assimilation through education remains a flashpoint shaping long-term regional stability.
insights.locator: Broader society in the region is conservative

insights.claim: Violence dropped noticeably by 2014 after peace talks between the BRN and the Thai military began in 2013, but years without breakthroughs let it creep back up, with mediator Srisompob Jitpiromsri saying the dialogue had no tangible results.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Talks alone reduce violence only temporarily; without concessions the risk resurfaces.
insights.quote: “The peace dialogue didn’t have any tangible effects or results,” Jitpiromsri said. “Just meeting and talk, talk.”
insights.locator: By 2014, there was a noticeable drop

insights.claim: Jitpiromsri says Thaksin Shinawatra was more open to concessions but had no power over the armed forces, while the current military-aligned government is less open to compromise.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Civil-military alignment now cuts against compromise, lowering near-term odds of a peace deal.
insights.locator: Jitpiromsri, of Deep South Watch, said

insights.claim: The conservative Bhumjaithai Party rode surging nationalism to victory in Thailand's February 2026 elections after conflict on the Cambodian border, and many residents of the deep south fear violence will escalate under the new pro-military government.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: A nationalist turn in Bangkok raises the probability of heavier-handed security policy and regional instability.

insights.claim: Nachemson expects military reprisals to rise alongside separatist violence, particularly as the military suspects some political figures of secretly coordinating with the BRN, citing a March 2026 drive-by shooting of a Muslim MP by former military personnel.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: A reprisal cycle targeting politicians would deepen political risk in southern Thailand.
insights.quote: As separatist violence ticks up again, it’s likely that military reprisals will, too

insights.claim: Most people Foreign Policy interviewed in the deep south expect the situation to keep deteriorating, with activist Artef Sohko warning that the absence of political space will push youth toward the BRN and armed groups.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Closing nonviolent channels raises insurgent recruitment and the longevity of the conflict.
insights.quote: “There’s no political space,” Sohko said. “It makes people lose faith. It will make the youth turn to BRN, turn to the armed groups.”
insights.locator: Most of those whom Foreign Policy spoke

insights.claim: The Thai government sometimes shuts down nonviolent paths to change, as with the sedition trial of activist Artef Sohko of the nonviolent group The Patani over a university talk on independence.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Prosecuting peaceful advocacy signals a securitized approach likely to sustain the insurgency.
insights.quote: This sometimes means the government shuts down non-violent pathways for change.

insights.claim: Soraya Jamjuree notes the Thai military isolates families of slain insurgents, denying them financial support and scholarships mandated for other victims' children, which raises the chance the next generation is recruited.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Exclusionary policy perpetuates the conflict across generations.
insights.locator: To some observers, the cycle of violence

insights.claim: The BRN's sometimes wanton violence can backfire on the insurgency, as shown by a 10-year-old Malay Muslim victim of the July attack who now wants to join the Thai Navy.
insights.speaker: Andrew Nachemson
insights.so_what: Insurgent violence against civilians can erode local support, a modest counterweight to escalation.
